I think I would push back on the idea that credit and debit cards represent a deadweight loss to the economy. Operating a cash business has its own expenses - theft risk (employee or otherwise), handling time, and (most importantly) you are limiting your customer base to only cash. There's a lot of reasons lots of small businesses are going card only. For good or bad, a lot of studies have confirmed that cards have overwhelmingly increased consumer spending. I think the far stronger case is that the industry has no actual incentive to fix the underlying fraud that they are charging merchants to fight. They have done a lot of work to institutionalize the problematic infrastructure and make it almost impossible for startups or outsiders to fix.

FedNow charges $0.045 per transaction and runs 24/7 and payments are instant. A better solution would be bank cards that used the FedNow network already in place which would send money directly to the merchant, bypassing visa/mastercard entirely. I've been using Same Day ACH in all my businesses for over a decade and the transaction fees are about $0.30/transaction and the dispute window is 60 days for PPD (personal checking accounts) and 3 days for CCD (commercial check accounts) and you get the money the same day. It beats paying visa/mastercard percentage fees and the 120 day dispute windows where people can literally get their money back four months later for work that was already performed. By using Same Day ACH, we get the money from the customer faster, save potentially millions of dollars in fees, and reduce dispute windows from four months to 3 days (for B2B sales)

Basic reforms that could solve this problem: 1. Merchants need to be allowed to add card processing fees on top of any transaction, and it should be possible to do this very easily. If not this, then any receipt should be required to include card processing fees. 2. Merchants should be allowed to pick and choose which cards they accept without penalty. Those two simple changes would add competitive pressure back into the payment processing market, and quickly cause fees to lower.

This article is full of mistakes and misleading claims: 1) It's claiming SHA1 insecurity is theoretical, while SHAttered from 2017 was specifically a pratical proof of concept. The only reason Git wasn't affected, is because they didn't bother bruteforcing a git-blob prefix. 2) It's claiming collision attacks don't matter, only second-preimage attacks do. This is incorrect, collision attacks are enough for code-smuggling problems, when two repositories are on the same git commit (verified by the full commit hash), yet contain different code in their git checkout. 3) The Linus quote "The real security is in distribution" is arguing that "git's content-addressed system should not be used to address content". It's arguing that, in case of curl|sh, you shouldn't use a sha256sum-gate to pin the content to something you've reviewed, you should instead ensure curl is fetching from an https server.

The first reason the author lists for why this will be bad is only an "issue" on Git hosts that don't allow repo creation on push (which is brain dead of GitHub). Any other host, you push your new repo, and it will see the hashing algorithm, and receive the contents accordingly. Submodules is a legitimate argument against this, though I don't know how widely this feature is actually used, and similar to the arguments in favor of switching the default branch from master to main, this is simply a setting which can be changed. I do like the idea of commits having both hashes, and am surprised that idea has not been explored further. Generally though, I think the author's strongest argument is simply that the change isn't strictly "needed", and all the other issues presented aren't the strongest arguments against change.

> We can go through years of this SHA-1 to SHA-256 migration and then quantum computers break 256 and we're back in the same stupid boat again. SHA-256 is considered quantum safe by the NIST and is left out of PQC migration guidance entirely.

Can someone more cyber-pilled than me explain what the actual risk with Git hashes being susceptible to collision attacks is? Obviously accidental collisions are problematic, but to my understanding the probability of that is still approximately zero. Best I can tell, all a forced collision would do is let someone who already has control of a repo modify the history in a far from plausibly deniable way. Which in practical terms, they already could do simply by replacing the whole thing, because who's out here using git hashes as a security tool? Every pinning I've ever seen has been to tags (which can be modified at will), or hashes of the actual payload (which doesn't need to be the same as what git uses).

One thing I've been thinking about is Baumol's Cost Disease. It's usually applied in at a macro scale across an economy: when a job somewhere becomes much more efficient, it makes all other jobs comparatively more expensive. I've started to notice this on a micro scale as well. I am 20x more productive at coding and scripting, but I don't spend more of my time coding. My time is now filled with things like presentations, Jira, QA, etc. Ironically, despite all of the automation, the things that are painstaking and time consuming disproportionately require more time now.
Just counting by hours is not reflecting the impact on the economy. Treemap weighted by GDP will make more sense.

I think “covered well” is being used here as a synonym for “covered at all”. For example, the “social workers & care -> counsel parents with child rearing problems” category is considered “well covered” because there are 13 prompts. It’s self-evident that the spectrum of work carried out by a social worker undertaking that work cannot be well represented by thirteen prompts. I suspect if you really strictly defined “covered well”, to the extent that any normal person would use that phrase, the headline would be above 99.9%.

Based on my own experience working on AI-based solutions for one of the better-covered job families according to this map, I think 90% might be overstating the case. It's true that we've got a lot of published benchmarks, but they tend to cover the lowest value add tasks. It's really easy to fall into the McNamara fallacy when rolling out these kinds of solutions. Focusing on the low value stuff is attractive. It tends to be easier to do, and also easier to quantify outcomes. But it also tends to direct attention away from important but difficult to quantify considerations, which may mean you don't notice negative externalities. So we often found ourselves in a verschilmmbessern situation where automating what we could automate made things worse overall.

It's time for the rest of the world to learn about Amdahl's Law. Even if we flipped a switch and tomorrow everything that could reasonably done by AI was suddenly free and instantaneous, the world does not instantly transform into an AI paradise wonderland of free goodies and lollipops because there's still plenty of other things that need to be done for goodie and lollipop production and distribution. I guess if I wanted to put my skepticism about the AI stock bubble into one little phrase, it would be that I don't think the bubble has accounted for Amdahl's Law. Costs don't actually go to zero with AI, and there's a huge difference between costs falling even 90% and costs falling a full 100%. And the difference between "30% improvement this year, trending to 85% in five years" and "90% this year" is pretty significant too.
